title: Short Links for Private Campaigns
prompt: An agency creates short links for its clients' campaigns. Some campaigns are private, so their codes must not be guessable. Design the shortener using the full routine.
facts: About 50 million new links a month, each opened about 50 times on average; peaks of 10,000 redirects per second
Links are kept for 3 years; a link record is about 500 bytes

Generated codes are 7 base62 characters (62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion). Public campaigns may instead ask for a custom name of 8 to 30 characters, such as summer-sale-2027; private campaigns always get generated codes

Measured on a test setup at the 10,000 per second peak: when shared caches may keep a redirect for 60 seconds, the CDN answers about 90% of redirects; an app server answers a redirect within 10 ms from its cache and within 30 ms from the database; the database has 4 shards, each with one replica, and each copy handles about 5,000 lookups per second; the app servers together handle about 15,000 redirects per second
A library is available that maps every number from 0 to 62⁷ − 1 to a different 7-character code, one to one, in an order that looks random to anyone without its secret key
Requirement: no two links ever share a code, and a private campaign's generated codes cannot be guessed from other codes
Requirement: a change of destination takes effect within 10 minutes; click counts appear within 15 minutes; a redirect takes under 50 ms inside the system
scope: Creating links, redirecting, changing destinations and counting clicks
Billing clients and checking for harmful sites are out of scope

requirements: States no shared codes, unguessable codes for private campaigns with custom names only for public ones, changes within 10 minutes, clicks within 15 minutes, redirects under 50 ms, 3 years of links
estimation: Traffic: 50 million ÷ 2.6 million ≈ 19 creations per second; 2.5 billion redirects a month ≈ 960 per second on average, 10,000 at peak; with the CDN answering 90%, about 1,000 per second reach the servers
Storage: 50 million × 12 × 3 = 1.8 billion links × 500 bytes ≈ 900 GB in 4 shards; with random codes, a new code repeats an old one at most about 1.8 billion ÷ 3.5 trillion ≈ 1 in 1,900
design: API (create, change, redirect), a data model with the code as primary key, a high-level design with a CDN and a cache on the redirect path, and a deep dive on making codes without collisions and on the redirect status code
data: Codes: random with the unique key catching repeats, or numbers from ranges mapped through the one-to-one library; custom names, for public campaigns only, in the same table under the same unique key
Redirect: 302, with headers that make browsers check again before reusing it and let the CDN keep it briefly, so changes and clicks are seen
tradeoffs: Names failures with conditions and a trade-off, such as: random codes need a retry on the rare repeat; ranges need a service that hands them out; a longer CDN time saves load but delays changes; a summary that checks each requirement

fullMarkDesigns: Design A, random codes. Requirements: create links (custom names for public campaigns only), redirect within 50 ms, change destinations within 10 minutes, count clicks within 15 minutes, never share a code, unguessable codes for private campaigns, keep 3 years; out of scope: billing, harmful-site checks. Estimates: about 19 creations and 960 redirects per second on average, 10,000 at peak, of which about 1,000 reach the servers; 1.8 billion links ≈ 900 GB. API: POST /links {longUrl, name?} → {code}; PATCH /links/{code} {longUrl}; GET /{code} → 302. Data: links(code primary key, long_url, owner, private, created_at) in 4 shards by code; clicks(code, day, count). High-level: creations go through the app servers to the shard; redirects go CDN → app servers → app cache → shard on a miss; clicks go to a queue. Deep dive: the server inserts 7 random base62 characters as the primary key; the unique key rejects a repeat (at most about 1 in 1,900) and the server tries again; a taken custom name is refused, and private campaigns cannot ask for one. Redirects answer 302 with Cache-Control: max-age=0, s-maxage=60, so browsers check again before reusing it and the CDN keeps it 60 seconds; app cache entries expire within 8 minutes, so a change shows within 10. Failures: a shard's replica serves redirects if its main copy fails; if the app cache is lost, about 1,000 per second go to the shards, about 250 each, within 5,000; if the CDN fails, 10,000 per second reach the app servers, within their 15,000. Summary: unique key for N3, random codes and no custom names for private campaigns, 30 ms redirects with 90% at the CDN, 302 with short cache times for changes, clicks from the queue and CDN logs within 15 minutes. Trade-off: a retry on the rare repeat.

Design B, ranges and the one-to-one library. Requirements and estimates as in Design A: custom names for public campaigns only; about 19 creations and up to 10,000 redirects per second, about 1,000 at the servers; about 900 GB. API: the same three calls. Data: the same links and clicks tables, plus ranges(server, next, end) in a small range service. High-level: each app server asks the range service for a block of 10,000 numbers and turns each number into a code with the library; redirects and clicks follow the same path as in Design A. Deep dive: numbers are never handed out twice and the library is one to one, so generated codes never collide, and without its key they look random, so private campaigns' codes cannot be guessed; custom names are 8 or more characters, so they never equal a 7-character code, and the unique key refuses a taken name. Redirects use 302 with max-age=0, s-maxage=60 and app cache entries expiring within 8 minutes, so changes show within 10 minutes. Failures: if the range service is down, servers keep creating from their current block; shard, cache and CDN failures as in Design A, within the measured capacities. Summary: no repeats by construction, unguessable private codes, the same redirect, change and click guarantees. Trade-off: one more service to run, and a server that crashes wastes the rest of its block.

assumptions: The measured CDN share holds at peak
The library's secret key is kept in a secret store (SD 13)
reference.design:
Requirements: create links, with custom names for public campaigns only, redirect under 50 ms, change destinations within 10 minutes, count clicks within 15 minutes, never share a code, unguessable codes for private campaigns, keep links 3 years.
Estimates: about 19 creations and 960 redirects per second on average, 10,000 at peak, of which the CDN answers about 90%, so about 1,000 reach the servers; 1.8 billion links × 500 bytes ≈ 900 GB in 4 shards.
API: POST /links {longUrl, name?} → {code}; PATCH /links/{code}; GET /{code} → 302. Data: links(code primary key, long_url, owner, created_at), sharded by code; clicks per link and day.
Design and deep dive: the server inserts 7 random base62 characters as the primary key; a repeat, at most about 1 in 1,900 near the end of 3 years, is rejected by the unique key, and the server tries again. Random codes cannot be guessed from others, and private campaigns cannot choose custom names. Custom names share the table and the unique key. Redirects answer 302 with Cache-Control: max-age=0, s-maxage=60, so browsers must check again before reusing the redirect and the CDN keeps it 60 seconds; app cache entries expire within 8 minutes, so a change shows within 10 minutes. A 301 would let browsers keep old destinations and hide clicks.
Redirects take at most 30 ms at the servers, within 50 ms.
Failures and summary: a shard's replica serves redirects if its main copy fails; if the app cache is lost, about 1,000 per second reach the shards, about 250 each, within 5,000; if the CDN fails, 10,000 per second reach the app servers, within their 15,000. Clicks are counted every few minutes from a queue and the CDN's logs, within 15 minutes.
alternatives: Numbers from ranges mapped through the one-to-one library: no collisions and not guessable, with a range service to run
Rejected: a plain counter in base62, because codes would be guessable and private pages could be found
Rejected: 301 redirects, because browsers would keep old destinations and clicks would not be seen
